history_of_present_illness: Tularaemia in man is typically characterized by a punched-out ulcer at the site of a bite, associated with swelling and suppuration of the glands draining the affected area. Local lesions are generally observed about the head or on parts of the body not covered by clothing. The disease has a sudden onset, often with chilliness or rigors, followed by dizziness, prostration, malaise, headache, and pains in the back and limbs. An irregular fever course typically lasts three or four weeks. Rhinitis and epistaxis may occur. Prostration is a main feature and continues marked during the several weeks or months of convalescence. Laboratory workers may experience infections without local signs. In some cases, conjunctival ulcerations with glandular involvement have been noted. A second attack of the disease, observed in one individual, presented with a papule on a finger and subsequent involvement of epitrochlear and axillary glands, but without fever or malaise, indicating a degree of immunity.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Tularaemia is a plague-like disease primarily affecting various rodents, such as jack rabbits and ground squirrels, and is transmissible to man. The causative organism is *Bacterium tularense*. The disease is prevalent in jack rabbits in Utah, where transmission to humans is often through the bite of an infected horsefly (*Chrysops discalis*) that has previously fed on infected jack rabbits. Cases have also been reported in the middle west due to handling infected rabbits. The first human infection was reported from Ohio in 1914. Subsequently, cases have been noted among rural residents of Utah and laboratory workers handling infected animals. The infection of ground squirrels was noted in California. Other vectors identified experimentally include the squirrel flea, house fly (*Musca domestica*), stable fly (*Stomoxys calcitrans*), rabbit louse (*Haemodipsus ventricosus*), mouse louse, and bedbug. Transmission by lice occurs from rabbit to rabbit and among white mice. Bedbugs can transmit the infection through bites, by feeding on infected bedbugs, and their faeces are infectious. Mice fed on the liver of an infected rabbit can also succumb. *Chrysops discalis* is considered the common transmitting agent for human infection, with sick and dying jack rabbits serving as the primary reservoir. Tularaemia chiefly affects the rural population working in fields. Laboratory workers carrying out extensive animal experimentation with *B. tularense* face a very high risk of infection, almost 100%. Natural reservoirs include ground squirrels in California and Utah, jack rabbits in Utah, and wild rabbits in the middle west. The infected deer fly (horsefly) is thought to be a mechanical transmitter, tending to lose infectivity after about five days.
vitals: During rigors, temperature may rapidly rise to 103° or 104°F, followed by an irregular fever course for two or three weeks. The pulse is rather rapid, and blood pressure is uninfluenced.
physical_exam: Physical examination is almost invariably negative, with the spleen generally not palpable. Local lesions at the site of a fly-bite are common, often appearing as punched-out ulcers, associated with swelling and suppuration of adjoining lymph glands. In a second attack, a papule on a finger with subsequent involvement of the epitrochlear and axillary glands was noted. Conjunctival ulcerations with glandular involvement can also occur.
labs_and_diagnostics: *Bacterium tularense* is a small, nonmotile, Gram-negative cocco-bacillus, 0.3 to 0.7µ long, appearing to be surrounded by capsular material in stained preparations. It is very difficult to cultivate, traditionally grown on coagulated egg yolk medium; scant growth can occur on serum or blood agar, improved by adding a piece of fresh sterile spleen. It refuses to grow on ordinary media. In experimental animals, infection can be induced by rubbing culture material, pus from a bubo, or an emulsion of an infected guinea pig's spleen into abraded skin. Autopsy of infected guinea pigs shows hemorrhagic oedema at the inoculation site, caseation of lymph glands, and small necrotic foci in the spleen and liver. Smears from the spleen show varying numbers of organisms. Bacteriaemia is common in infected rodents but only rarely found in human blood. White and differential blood counts vary little from normal. For diagnosis, material from ulcers or glands should be inoculated into guinea pigs or white mice, as human blood cultures or animal inoculations from human blood are almost always negative. Complement fixation and agglutination tests are reliable diagnostic methods. An antigen for these tests is prepared by washing off a 72-hour growth from egg yolk medium with saline, heating for 30 minutes at 56°C, and preserving with 0.3% tricresol.
differential_diagnosis: The disease is described as a 'plague-like disease' in rodents, and experimentally induced lesions in animals cannot be well differentiated from those of plague. In humans, the mental state (practically no apathy) helps differentiate it from typhoid fever and the marked clouding of consciousness seen in plague.
management_and_clinical_course: Tularaemia is rarely fatal but is a most incapacitating disease due to a prolonged convalescence lasting three or four months, during which the patient's strength and energy are markedly affected. Treatment is entirely symptomatic. Patients who go to bed at once and remain there during the fever stage seem to be less seriously affected. Prophylaxis involves wearing rubber gloves when performing autopsies on experimentally infected animals due to the high risk of infection. Awareness and control of potential natural transmitters such as house flies, stable flies, horseflies, bedbugs, and lice, as well as the significant reservoirs in ground squirrels, jack rabbits, and wild rabbits, are crucial.
